newsitem.title: UK: OLYMPICS-IOC WARNS BIDDING CITIES ON COMMERCIALISM.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-IOC WARNS BIDDING CITIES ON COMMERCIALISM.

text.p: Olympic chiefs have warned the five cities bidding to host the 2004 Summer Games that the commercial excesses which sparked huge controversy at last year's Atlanta Olympics must never happen again.

International Olympic Committee (IOC) marketing director Michael Payne said on Wednesday the issue was a key part of a Tuesday meeting which the IOC held with the bidding cities -- Rome, Athens, Buenos Aires, Cape Town and Stockholm.
"The idea is to make sure the house is in order prior to the election (of the winning city in September)," Payne said from the IOC's headquarters in Switzerland.

"All the cities are aware that it was a PR own goal for the city of Atlanta. It is a matter of the whole image of the Games. The goal of the bidding candidates is to put their city in the best possible light."
Atlanta was heavily criticised for commercial excesses, especially the street vendors selling junk memorabilia.
Some said the large number of city-backed private vendors allowed to clog the city centre had made the Games look like a huge flea market.
The IOC has a number of official sponsors and rules about how the Olympic Games can be used in advertising.
Last year the organisation said it would be tightening its rules on commercialism and would not give the Games to cities in the future unless they agreed with its marketing plans.
The IOC told the bidding cities that the contract which the winning city will sign will be very clear about how the Olympic Games can be used in advertising.
Payne said the cities supported the action completely.
"We are preaching to the converted," he said. "They know they have to take the administrative steps to avoid local misunderstandings on this."
Payne said Sydney, which hosts the next Summer Games in the year 2000, had already introduced even tougher rules on commercialism than the IOC requires.
"They are so anxious that the city is not going to be mis-represented and that is music to our ears," he said.
